To vend means to sell something, particularly by offering it to people in a public setting. Think of someone standing at a stall, a cart, or a booth and handing products to customers in exchange for money. That act — that specific kind of selling — is what "vend" captures.

So to vend = to sell.
But Isn't It Just "Sell"? What Makes "Vend" Special?

Yes, "vend" and "sell" overlap, but "vend" carries a slightly more specific and formal flavor. Here's the difference:

"Sell" is a broad, everyday word. You can sell your old bike to a friend, sell an idea to your boss, or sell a house. It covers almost any kind of exchange.

"Vend," on the other hand, leans toward selling goods directly to the public, often in an open, accessible, or physical setting — like a street, a market, a machine, or a roadside stall. It paints a picture of a vendor (a seller) presenting products openly for anyone to come and buy.

You wouldn't naturally say someone "vended" a house or "vended" an idea. The word fits best when real, physical goods are being offered to the general public.

1. Street and market selling
When someone sets up a cart on a sidewalk and sells food, trinkets, or newspapers, they are vending those goods. The people who do this are called vendors — a word you've almost certainly heard before.

The man vended fresh fruit from a wooden cart every morning.

2. Vending machines
This is probably the most familiar context. A vending machine vends — it sells items automatically when you insert money and press a button. The machine is, quite literally, a mechanical vendor. The word "vending" in "vending machine" is just the verb "vend" in action.

The machine on the corner vends cold drinks and snacks.

3. Formal and legal writing
In official documents, business writing, or legal texts, "vend" is sometimes used instead of "sell" to sound precise and formal.

The company was licensed to vend its products in three countries.

In older or very formal usage, "vend" has occasionally been used to mean to express or spread an opinion or idea publicly — almost like putting your thoughts "up for sale" in the marketplace of public discussion. However, this usage is rare and largely outdated today. You are very unlikely to encounter it in modern writing. When you see "vend" in any current context, it almost always means to sell.
Words That Come From "Vend" (You'll See These Often)

Since you'll encounter these closely related words in real life, knowing their connection to "vend" helps everything click together.

Vendor — a person or company that vends (sells) goods. Street food vendor, software vendor, a vendor at a fair — all sellers.

Vending — the act of selling, as in "vending machine" (a machine that does the selling for you).

Vendible — an adjective meaning something that is fit or suitable to be sold; sellable. Less common, but you may see it in formal contexts.

Vend itself is also used as a noun in some legal or commercial contexts, simply meaning "a sale."
A Quick Summary to Lock It In

To vend is to sell goods, especially directly to the public — think market stalls, street carts, and vending machines. It is more formal than "sell" and tends to suggest an open, accessible kind of selling where a vendor offers products to whoever comes along. The word is most commonly seen in everyday life through its relatives: vendor (the seller) and vending machine (the automated seller).

If you remember the vending machine, you'll never forget what "vend" means.
